blocks.text: Unless I am mistaken, doves of the trees, or of the groves, are also mentioned in the title [col. 18] of Psal. LVI., in the rendering of which I think interpreters have so far laboured in vain. For, to pass over the ancients, who go off in the most diverse directions, who could tolerate Selomo or Kimchi, who render the Hebrew words על יונת אלם רחוקים as concerning the dove of silence of those far off, [II, 547] so as to refer them to David? For, as Selomo says, David was then among the Philistines, far from the land of Israel. And Kimchi adds that he is called a dove because in Os. VII, 11. the dove is called silly, and David was feigning to be a fool; and a dove of silence, that is, mute, because he did not speak in his usual manner but like a madman. Nor do I much more approve of a great man ^{(2)} from among our own, who, following the authors of the Midrash, explains the same words thus: Concerning the soul suffering violence from a band of those far off. This interpretation, like the former one we have discussed, does such manifest violence to the Hebrew text that anyone even moderately learned in Hebrew will see why I reject it. Leaving these aside, then, I shall say what the matter is. Aben Ezra rightly saw that the words יונת אלם רחוקים are the opening of a song to whose melody David composed this Psalm; but he left them ἀνερμήνευτα [anermēneuta]. Here, however, we are asking what those words mean. And it is certain that no suitable sense can be drawn from them as they are read by the Masoretes. Let the experts therefore consider whether, keeping the same letters but changing one vowel point, it would not be wiser to read אלם elim instead of אלם elem, that is, Hirec for Segol. Granted this, the opening of the sacred song whose melody David follows in this Psalm would be: The dove of the distant groves. What misled the interpreters, and even the Masoretes themselves, is that אלם lacks the Iod, the mark of the plural. But, as the distinguished Buxtorf rightly observes in Thesaurus Grammaticus, book 1, ch. 9, Iod often drops out of the plural, as in תנינם, dragons, Deut. XXXII, 33., תמימם, unblemished, Levit. IX, 2. I add only an example of a similar ellipsis in this very word, though in another sense: באלם, among the mighty gods, for באלים, Exod. XV, 11. Further, יונת אלים, the dove of the trees, or of the groves, is the wild dove, that is, the wood pigeon (palumbus), which lives in woods and nests in trees. Theocritus, Idyll 5:
Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθω καθελών· τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφίσδει· [Kēgō men dōsō tai parthenōi autika phassan, Ek tas arkeuthō kathelōn; tēnei gar ephisdei]
And I will soon give the girl a wood pigeon, taken from the juniper: for there it sits. Nemesianus, Eclogue 2:
Besides, I have sent a tender hare and a pair of wood pigeons, the spoils of the woods, which I lately could.
The wood pigeon claps its wings, calling from the leafy tree.

Accordingly the French call it ramier, from the branches (rami) of the trees on which it perches. The same is written also of the rock doves (liviae), which the Greeks call πελειάδες [peleiades]. Thus Herodotus in Euterpe describes a πελειάδα [peleiada], a rock dove, ἰζομένην ἐπὶ φηγὸν [izomenēn epi phēgon], perching on a beech. And of the turtledove Origen [II, 548] on the Song of Songs, Homily 2: It always lingers on the ridges of mountains and on the tops of trees. Theodoret also, on Cant. 2, says that the turtledove ἐν δένδροις ἀμφιλαφέσι τὰς καλιὰς πηγνύναι [en dendrois amphilaphesi tas kalias pēgnynai], builds its nests in shady trees. And Chrysostom in the homily On the Turtledove: Ἐπὶ τῶν στερεμνίων πρέμνων τὴν καλίαν αὐτῶν πήξασαι, καὶ ἀφόβως ἐπωάζουσαι, τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἑαυτῶν ἐκεῖθεν πετάζουσι· [Epi tōn steremniōn premnōn tēn kalian autōn pēxasai, kai aphobōs epōazousai, tous neottous heautōn ekeithen petazousi] Fixing their nest on firm tree trunks and brooding securely, they spread out their young there. This is infrequent in doves properly so called, yet not without example. Hence Anacreon, Ode 9, says that a περιστερὰν [peristeran] πέτασθαι ὄρη τε, καὶ κατ᾽ ἄγρους, καὶ δένδρεσιν καθίζειν [petasthai orē te, kai kat' agrous, kai dendresin kathizein], flies over mountains and fields and perches on trees. And Horace, book 1, Ode 2:
And the race of fishes clung to the top of the elm, which had been the familiar seat of doves.
And Virgil in book 6, of the doves sent to Aeneas by Venus:
They settle in the longed-for seat upon the twofold tree. [col. 19]

And Suetonius in the Octavius, ch. 94, on the palm near Munda which the deified Julius had ordered to be preserved as an omen of victory: From it a shoot at once sprang up and in a few days grew so much that it not only equalled the parent tree but even overshadowed it, and was frequented by the nests of doves, although that kind of bird especially avoids hard and rough foliage. From these it is plain what the dove of the trees, or of the distant groves, in the title of the Psalm is: namely, distant from cities and cultivated places ^{(3)}.
